claims.claim: Maths anxiety is reliably and negatively related to maths performance in school-aged students, and the link is stronger at secondary age than at primary age, so it deserves to be measured rather than assumed absent.
claims.source_title: The Relation Between Mathematics Anxiety and Mathematics Performance Among School-Aged Students: A Meta-Analysis
claims.key_numbers: 131 studies, 478 effect sizes; pooled r = -0.34; primary grades r = -0.27, secondary grades r = -0.36; moderated by MA dimension, task difficulty and effects on grades (Review of Educational Research 89(3), 459-496)
claims.implication: Nothing in the tracker or skills records how anxious the student is about maths. A one-item, optional self-rating (e.g. 1-5 'how worried are you about maths today') captured at the start of timed work or a mock, and reviewed next to the existing 'blanks per paper' metric, would let the parent see whether blank answers track anxiety or track skill gaps.

claims.claim: A second, larger meta-analysis puts the maths-anxiety/achievement correlation in the small-to-moderate range (about r = -0.28), so anxiety is a real but partial explanation for poor maths performance and should not displace skill gaps as the main lever.
claims.source_title: A meta-analysis of the relation between math anxiety and math achievement
claims.key_numbers: 223 studies; pooled r approximately -0.28; samples from grade 1 to non-student adults; country estimates range from r = -0.54 (Turkey, India) to r = -0.12 (Indonesia); Psychological Bulletin 147(2), 134-168
claims.implication: With 24 not-started and 12 gap topics in maths, the plan's priority on coverage is correct; anxiety-reduction routines should sit alongside, not ahead of, closing the Foundation-first gaps (G1, G3, P4-P8, S2, S4) in the review queue.

claims.claim: Students with an ADHD diagnosis reported higher maths anxiety than peers without a diagnosis even though the two groups did not differ on arithmetic performance, so good scores on a check do not rule out maths anxiety in an ADHD learner.
claims.source_title: History of ADHD traits related to general test and specific math anxiety in college students
claims.authors_year: authors not shown in search summary; 2017 (Learning and Individual Differences)
claims.key_numbers: ADHD-diagnosed group higher on math anxiety, no difference on arithmetic performance; ADHD symptoms correlated with all anxiety measures; exact effect sizes not shown in search summary; sample was college students, not 13-year-olds
claims.implication: The 22/25, zero-blank exit check on 19 Aug should not be read as 'anxiety solved'. The maths-tutor-session rule 'if frustrated pause and suggest a break' should be widened to an explicit check-in before any timed or mock work, and the answer logged in the session summary so the parent can see a trend.

claims.claim: Anxiety disorders co-occur with ADHD in roughly one in five children and adolescents, so the parent should be alert to clinically significant anxiety rather than treating exam nerves as ordinary.
claims.source_title: Psychiatric comorbidity in children and adolescents with ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis
claims.authors_year: authors not shown in search summary; 2025 (Clinical Psychology Review)
claims.key_numbers: Anxiety disorders 18.4% comorbid (also ODD 34.7%, behaviour disorders 30.7%, specific phobias 11.0%); other sources in the same search give a 17-25% range for anxiety-ADHD co-occurrence
claims.implication: The brief records no information on diagnosis, medication or comorbidities. Before the Dec 2026 mock the parent should decide whether anxiety has ever been assessed, because a comorbid anxiety disorder would change how mocks are run (shorter, lower-stakes, more frequent) and what access arrangements to seek from the exam centre.

claims.claim: The ADHD-maths link is driven more by inattention than by hyperactivity/impulsivity, with twin studies showing a genetic correlation between maths and ADHD that is larger for the inattentive component.
claims.source_title: A systematic review of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and mathematical ability: current findings and future implications
claims.authors_year: Tosto, Momi, Asherson & Malki, 2015 (BMC Medicine, not Frontiers in Psychology)
claims.key_numbers: Genetic correlation greater for inattentive than hyperactive-impulsive component; magnitudes not shown in search summary
claims.implication: Treat 'not reading the question', answering parts that were not asked, and losing place in multi-step work as inattention-driven failure modes, not laziness or motivation. The tracker should record a 'read-the-question' or 'answered wrong part' error category separately from knowledge gaps so the pattern can be seen across topics rather than buried in free-text watch notes.

claims.claim: In children with and without ADHD, both parent- and teacher-rated inattention symptoms are significantly correlated with maths achievement, so day-to-day attention state is a plausible predictor of session outcomes.
claims.source_title: Neurocognitive and Behavioral Predictors of Math Performance in Children with and without ADHD
claims.authors_year: Antonini et al., c. 2016 (authors from memory; not shown in search summary)
claims.key_numbers: Inattention ratings significantly correlated with math achievement; coefficients not shown in search summary
claims.implication: Because the tracker records neither time of day nor session length nor how a session ended, the parent cannot tell whether poor sessions follow poor attention. Adding a two-field 'started at / ended how (finished, ran out, stopped)' record to log_session would make this checkable.

claims.claim: Working memory, especially the central executive, mediates the applied (multi-step, word-problem) maths difficulties of children with ADHD, so problems that require holding several steps in mind are where this student is most at risk.
claims.source_title: Applied Problem Solving in Children with ADHD: The Mediating Roles of Working Memory and Mathematical Calculation
claims.authors_year: Friedman et al., 2017/2018 (authors from memory; not shown in search summary)
claims.key_numbers: Mediation by working memory and calculation reported; path coefficients not shown in search summary. A companion APA Neuropsychology study (https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/features/neu-neu0000920.pdf) used bifactor modelling of central executive, visuospatial and phonological components against computation, problem-solving and fluency in children with and without ADHD; effect sizes not shown
claims.implication: Submitting answers without working (twice on 2 Sep) is a working-memory risk, not only a lost-marks risk: the tutor skill should require each intermediate step to be written before offering the next hint, and fill-in widgets that let arithmetic be done in prose (the frequency-tree case) should be replaced by ones that make each number visible on the page.

claims.claim: A brief, explicit planning-strategy routine for maths (ten days of PASS-based cognitive strategy instruction) produced large gains for students with ADHD that transferred to standardised maths tests and persisted at one year, so teaching a fixed 'plan, do, check' routine is worth the session time.
claims.source_title: A cognitive strategy instruction to improve math calculation for children with ADHD and LD: a randomized controlled study
claims.key_numbers: Randomised by classroom; 10 days of instruction; pre-post effect sizes experimental vs comparison: math worksheets 0.85 vs 0.26, Math Fluency 1.17 vs 0.09, Numerical Operations 0.40 vs -0.14; experimental group still ahead at 1-year follow-up
claims.implication: Script a fixed metacognitive sequence into the maths-tutor-session starter and exit ticket (what is the question asking, what do I know, which method, write each step, check the answer against the question) and run it for two weeks rather than relying on ad hoc hints; this directly targets the answer-targeting habit and the sign/collecting-terms slips on A4.

claims.claim: High-school students with ADHD attempted a similar number of test items and reported similar test anxiety and strategy use as peers, but were less accurate, which shows that leaving answers blank is not an inevitable ADHD trait and that accuracy after attempting is the next thing to watch.
claims.source_title: Test-taking performance of high school students with ADHD
claims.authors_year: Lewandowski et al., 2012/2013 (authors from memory; not shown in search summary)
claims.key_numbers: ADHD group had poorer decoding, comprehension and vocabulary accuracy; groups similar on reading speed, items attempted, perceived test anxiety, self-perceived testing skill and strategy use; magnitudes not shown; task was a reading test, not maths
claims.implication: The fall in blanks from 27/39 marks lost on Paper 3F to zero on the 19 Aug exit check is consistent with blanks being a modifiable behaviour. Keep 'blanks per paper' as the tracked metric, but add 'marks lost on attempted questions' so the progress report can show whether the 'write something down' script is producing marks or only ink.

claims.claim: Maths-anxious students avoid effortful study strategies when left to choose, so a student who says 'skip it' or 'I can't' should have practice assigned by the system rather than self-selected.
claims.source_title: Math Anxiety Predicts the Avoidance of Effortful Study Strategies
claims.authors_year: Jenifer et al., 2022 (authors from memory; not shown in search summary)
claims.implication: The review-queue-first opening in maths-tutor-session is the right design: the queue, not the student, should pick the hard topic. Where a question is abandoned (Q4/Q5 not submitted on 2 Sep) the skill should re-queue it explicitly rather than let it lapse.

claims.claim: Maths-anxiety interventions have been pooled in a published meta-analysis, so if anxiety is confirmed the parent has an evidence base to draw on, but the pooled effect size could not be read from the search summary and should be checked before investing session time.
claims.source_title: A Meta-Analysis of Math Anxiety Interventions
claims.authors_year: Balt et al., c. 2022 (authors from memory; not shown in search summary)
claims.implication: Do not build an anxiety-intervention feature into the skills yet; first confirm anxiety is present (C1, C3) and then read this meta-analysis for which intervention types (reappraisal, expressive writing, exposure to timed practice) carry the largest effects.

claims.claim: Inattention weakens the effect of a maths intervention in low-performing pupils, so the gains from a tutoring session are likely smaller when attention is poor, which argues against stacking two 90-minute sessions in one day.
claims.source_title: Inattention negatively moderates the effectiveness of a mathematics intervention in low performing primary school students
claims.authors_year: authors not shown in search summary; 2024 (Frontiers in Education)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary; sample was primary-school pupils with inattention symptoms, not diagnosed ADHD adolescents
claims.implication: Two full sessions were run on 2 Sep. The skill should cap full sessions at one per day and log session start/end so the parent can see whether second-session or late-day work produces more slips (A4 sign errors recur across three sessions).

claims.claim: A study has specifically classified the types of maths error made by adolescents with and without ADHD, so an error taxonomy for this student can be borrowed rather than invented, but its results were not visible in the search summary.
claims.source_title: Math Error Types and Correlates in Adolescents with and without Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
claims.authors_year: Capodieci & Martinussen, 2017 (authors from memory; not shown in search summary)
claims.implication: The parent should read this paper before building a 'mistake journal': the marker skills already produce a 'where you lost marks' table, and tagging each lost mark with an error type (misread question, sign/arithmetic slip, procedural, blank) taken from the paper would make error analysis a tracked field rather than free text.

claims.claim: AQA GCSE maths mark schemes award method marks for correct working even when the final answer is wrong and there is no negative marking, so an attempted question can never score below a blank; this is stated from general knowledge of AQA 8300 mark schemes and was not confirmed by search this session because the search budget was exhausted.
claims.source_title: no source retrieved this session (AQA 8300 mark schemes held by the gcse-maths-marker skill should be used to verify)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary; the system's own data show Paper 3F (Jul 2026) lost 27 of 39 marks to blanks and the 19 Aug exit check had zero blanks
claims.implication: The 'what's one thing you could write down?' script rests on this. Verify it against a published AQA mark scheme, then make the marker skills report method marks earned on wrong-answer questions as a separate figure so the student can see that partial working paid.

caveats: The session-wide WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted after this agent's 7th successful search; 8 further planned searches were refused. Topics NOT searched and therefore absent or unsourced: worked examples and cognitive-load effect sizes for showing working; learning-from-errors / erroneous-examples / mistake-journal meta-analyses; timed versus untimed practice and time-pressure effects on maths anxiety; extended-time accommodation evidence for ADHD; check-your-answer / self-monitoring interventions for ADHD in maths; the AQA method-marks policy document; the 'Confidence is key' ADHD-maths self-efficacy paper.
Only 7 successful searches were run, one short of the requested 8; this is a budget constraint, not a choice.
Author names marked '(from memory)' were not visible in the search summaries; titles and URLs were. A verification agent should confirm authorship before the report cites them by name.

C3 (ADHD and maths anxiety) is a college-student sample; C12 is primary-school and uses inattention symptoms rather than diagnosed ADHD; C9 used a reading test, not maths. None of the ADHD-specific evidence found was on 13-year-olds sitting maths exams.
Effect sizes for C5, C6, C7, C10, C11, C12 and C13 could not be read from the search summaries; those claims are directional only.

No study on 'blank answers' or item omission as a specific ADHD exam behaviour was found; the only direct evidence (C9) suggests items-attempted did not differ by ADHD status in that sample. The strongest evidence on blanks in this report is the system's own before/after data, which is a single-student observation.
General-population maths-anxiety correlations (C1, C2) may be inflated or deflated in an ADHD sample; no ADHD-specific meta-analysis of maths anxiety was found.
C14 is general knowledge, not a retrieved source, and is flagged as evidence_type 'none'.
